story.title: Investigation Launched into Alaska Senate Candidate Over Alleged Spoiler Scheme
story.summary: Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign. This follows allegations that her campaign recruited a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to confuse voters and dilute support for the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan. Donald Trump has also called for Peltola's prosecution over these claims.

event_overview.title: About Alaska Senate Race
event_overview.subject: Alaska Senate Race
event_overview.summary: The Alaska Senate race is the 2026 statewide contest for Alaska’s Class II seat in the U.S. Senate, held by Republican Dan Sullivan since 2015. It is part of the November 3, 2026, general election and is administered by the Alaska Division of Elections under the state’s nonpartisan top-four primary and ranked-choice general-election system.

facts.label: Election date
facts.value: Alaska’s 2026 general election, including the U.S. Senate contest, is scheduled for November 3, 2026.

facts.label: Office at stake
facts.value: The race is for one of Alaska’s two U.S. Senate seats: the Class II seat. The Senate lists Dan Sullivan as the current holder, and Class II terms expire in January 2027.

facts.label: Election administration
facts.value: The Alaska Division of Elections is the state body publishing the election calendar, candidate information, ballots, and voting guidance for the 2026 general election.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: Alaska uses a top-four primary: the four candidates receiving the most votes for an office advance to the general election, where voters may rank candidates. A candidate must ultimately receive a majority of counted votes to win.

facts.label: Candidate status
facts.value: The Division of Elections’ 2026 candidate materials identify certified U.S. Senate candidates and note that state and federal candidates who win their primary contests advance to the general election; official listings can change as filings, withdrawals, and certifications are processed.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows specific campaign-related developments, including candidate debate and allegation-related coverage, rather than providing a complete record of the election, every candidate activity, or final voting results.

explore_lenses.label: What did Dunleavy’s order actually change?
explore_lenses.title: A new state inquiry, not a ballot removal
explore_lenses.summary: Governor Mike Dunleavy directed Alaska’s Department of Public Safety to examine whether the alleged recruitment effort broke state law and could justify criminal charges or civil action. The order itself did not disqualify Mary Peltola or remove Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the ballot.

claims.text: Dunleavy said the Department of Public Safety should investigate whether the alleged scheme violated Alaska law and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.
Alaska’s official candidate list still showed Mary Peltola, incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as certified U.S. Senate candidates for the November 3, 2026 general election.

The state had previously investigated Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s filing and initially decertified him, citing evidence it said suggested an intent to confuse voters; subsequent court action restored his place on the ballot.

explore_lenses.label: What is the evidence—and how do the parties respond?
explore_lenses.title: Reported campaign links remain allegations
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate basis for the new inquiry is reporting that Peltola-aligned staff and Democratic operatives helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to divide the incumbent’s support. The campaign and national Democratic committee deny involvement, while a former campaign manager reportedly described Peltola as aware but not directly involved.

claims.text: The New York Times reporting cited by subsequent outlets was based on interviews, text messages, and documents that reportedly showed efforts to recruit candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to split support for the incumbent.

Former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios reportedly told the Times that Peltola was 'definitely aware' of the effort but was not directly involved; that account is a source’s characterization, not an adjudicated finding.

A Peltola campaign spokesperson said the campaign had no involvement with either Sullivan campaign, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee likewise denied involvement with Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
Sen. Dan Sullivan’s campaign said Alaskans deserve the truth and accused Peltola’s campaign of denying the alleged scheme.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next before and after Election Day?
explore_lenses.title: Two separate legal tracks are pending
explore_lenses.summary: The state investigation concerns possible responsibility for the alleged recruitment effort. Separately, the Justice Department has sued Alaska over post-election certification, seeking conditional relief if the incumbent loses by a margin that could be affected by votes for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

claims.text: The Justice Department’s federal lawsuit, filed October 22, seeks to delay certification only under specified conditions tied to a potential incumbent Sullivan loss and the number of votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.; it does not seek to stop voting before the November 3 election.
Alaska’s Department of Law has moved to dismiss the federal case, arguing that conditional delay of certification would interfere with state election administration and threaten election integrity.

Forecast: Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller told the Associated Press that the Justice Department case would likely apply only in a narrow-loss scenario and probably would not survive long in court.
Alaska’s official election-results page listed the November 3 general election as pending as of October 28 and describes the state’s ranked-choice tabulation process.

story_report.summary: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign after allegations that it sought to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whose name resembles that of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, to split voter support. Dunleavy directed the Department of Public Safety to determine whether Alaska law was violated and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. Former President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted, while her campaign denies involvement in either Sullivan campaign.

sections.heading: Campaign Accounts Conflict Over Recruitment
sections.body: Reporting cited by subsequent outlets said interviews, text messages and documents indicated efforts to recruit candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to draw support from the incumbent. Former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios reportedly told The New York Times that Peltola was “definitely aware” of the effort but not directly involved; that was a source characterization rather than an adjudicated finding. Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied involvement, while Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said voters deserve the truth.

sections.heading: Sullivan Ballot Status and Federal Case
sections.body: Alaska’s official candidate list still listed Peltola, Dan S. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as certified candidates for the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. The state previously investigated the junior Sullivan’s filing, initially decertified him over evidence it said suggested an intent to confuse voters, and later restored him to the ballot following court action. Separately, the Justice Department’s Oct. 22 lawsuit seeks to delay certification only under specified conditions tied to a possible Sullivan loss and votes cast for the other Sullivan; it does not seek to halt voting.

unresolved.text: It remains undetermined whether the state investigation will find a legal violation, whether charges or a civil case will follow, and whether a federal court will permit the requested conditional delay of election certification.
